item.title: Stats and Snaps – 2026 Week 1, Commanders @ Philadelphia Eagles
item.description: The Jones/Blough era gets off to a sputtering start
item.content:encoded:
Much has been made about the Commanders’ opening road loss to the 5.5-point favorite Philadelphia Eagles. While they did leave ample winning opportunities on the field, when the final whistle blew, the Commanders had held their top-ranked division rival to just 24 points and 318 total yards on offense. And, perhaps most importantly, they beat the spread.

While the opening day performance left plenty of room for improvement, their first game with new offensive and defensive schemes went better than might have been expected based on some of the doom and gloom prognostications making the rounds.

Against one of the better teams in the league, on the road, the Commanders offense ranked 17th in yardage gained and 20th in scoring; while the defense ranked 17th in yardage and 16th in score containment. Not top of the league table, but a fair bit better than the bottom of the league Week 1 power rankings might have suggested. 

In terms of offensive and defensive efficiency, as quantified by EPA/play, the Commanders and their opponents started their seasons right in the middle of the pack:

Graphic courtesy of RBSDM.com

Those looking for signs of hope for improvement this season might take inspiration from standout performances and flashes of potential by Pepsi Rookie of the Week winner WR Antonio Williams, LB Sonny Styles, 2026 FA additions Amik Robertson and Nick Cross, and special teams demon Tyler Owens, among others.

Now, let’s take an in-depth look at who stood out, who stood down, and who just stood around in the 22-24 road loss to the Eagles

Stats in this article were obtained from three main sources. Official stats from the NFL gamebook, are treated as a source of truth. Advanced stats (eg. pressures, yards before contact, yards allowed in coverage) were sourced from Pro Football Focus (PFF) and Pro Football Reference (PFR). Advanced stats rely on tape analysts’ judgement and often differ between services. Where there were differences, data from both sources is cited. When there was consensus, sources are not cited.

OFFENSE

Jayden Daniels’ stat line as a passer was an unimpressive 18 comp/34 att (52.9%) for 164 yds, 2 TDs and 0 INT. 

But there were really two parts to his game.  Through the first three quarters he looked off, as did his receivers.  His stat line at the end of the third quarter was 9 comp/23 att (39.1%) for 50 yds and 0 TD. In the fourth quarter, he locked in, throwing for 9/11 (81.8%) for 99 yds and 2 TDs.

According to PFR, his incompletions included 5 throw aways and 4 drops by receivers.  PFR counted pressure on 18.4% of dropbacks (NFL rank 23rd), which might have contributed to his 17.2% bad throw rate on passes which were not throw aways.

PFF has a lower threshold for recording pressures, making their pressure stats not comparable to PFR.  PFF counted 16 pressures (NFL rank 6; 42% of dropbacks).  His 1 sack taken gave him a respectable 6.3% pressure to sack rate. PFF counted 3 drops and 0 turnover-worthy passes.

On the ground, JD5 rushed 5 times for 31 yds (6.2 Y/A), including 3 scrambles, with 1 broken tackle, and 21 YAC per PFR (37 per PFF).

He was charged with delay of game penalties in the 2nd and 3rd quarters for 10 total yards.

Daniels’ 66.4 Total QBR ranked 14th in the NFL in Week 1.  Not terrible given the heavy pressure rate and all the drops by receivers. Hopefully the slow start was Jayden shaking off the rust of an injury-plagued 2025 season and lack of preseason snaps. If the fourth quarter was indicative of his performance in the new offense, or Blough adjusting the scheme to suit his QB, then the Cowboys could have their hands full.

Bill Croskey-Merritt led the Commanders’ rushing attack with 16 attempts for 63 yds (3.9 Y/A), 7 first downs, and 1 TD. His 50.0% rushing success rate ranked second on the team. PFF counted one forced missed tackle, but PFR did not. Bill had one fumble, fortunately recovered by teammate Josh Conerly. He caught one screen pass and was tackled 7 yards behind the line.

PFF recorded 1.25 YBC/att, just slightly below league average for RBs using 2025 stats. Like pressures, PFR uses a higher threshold for recording contact, making their numbers not comparable to PFF. According to PFR, Bill averaged 2.6 YBC/att, which is just below the 75th percentile for RBs based on 2025 figures. His room to run was therefore somewhere between league average and a little above average, depending on which stat service you believe.

Bill recorded his first career penalty, a 10 yd infraction for holding in pass protection.

Rachaad White rushed 7 times for 22 yds (3.1 Y/A) and 1 first down, with 1 broken tackle. His 42.9% success rate was the lowest on the team. He caught 2/2 passes for 5 total yds. PFF gave him more YBC/att (1.57 yds) than Bill, while PFR gave him fewer (2.0 yds), so it is difficult to know which to believe. 

Rookie Kaytron Allen had 4 carries for 16 yds (4.0 Y/A) in his NFL debut.  He led the team with a 100% rushing success rate.  He should be given more carries to see if he can keep that up.

In his NFL debut, Antonio Williams led Commanders’ receivers with 64 receiving yards, despite getting less than half the playing time of starter Terry McLaurin.  He caught 4/4 targets for 64 yds, 1 TD and 4 first downs (100% success rate) at an ADOT of 13.8 yds. His receiving productivity was in the elite range at 5.82 Y/RR, albeit on a very small sample of receiving snaps.

There was some question before the game about how David Blough might deploy the rookie WR. Williams took 15 snaps out wide and 11 in the slot. There is little question that he should get more playing time against the Cowboys. He was clearly Washington’s best receiver.

Stefon Diggs was second on the team with 55 receiving yds and 1 TD.  He had the same number of receptions as Williams (4), but more than twice as many targets, giving him the lowest reception rate on the team (44.4%). PFR credited Diggs with 3 drops in the game, equalling his season totals in 2025 and 2024. Even so, he was the Commanders’ second most productive receiver at a respectable 2.2 Y/RR.

Diggs’ game mirrored that of his QB to some extent. Through the first three quarters he caught 2/7 passes for 28 yds. In the fourth quarter, he caught 2/2 for 27 yds and a TD.

Compounding the slow start, Diggs’ game was also marred by an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty for 15 yards, following his 4th quarter TD to bring the score to 15 to 17. The gaffe moved the Commanders out of position to attempt a 2 pt conversion to tie the game.  

Terry McLaurin caught 2/4 targets for 14 yds. Jaylin Lane caught 1/1 targets for 4 yds. Dyami Brown failed to catch either of his two targets, albeit at a challenging ADOT of 31 yds.

Chig Okonkwo ushered in his Commanders’ tenure by catching 2/3 targets for 16 yards, including 1 contested catch.

John Bates also caught 2/3 targets, for a total of 13 yds. Bates got the lions’ share of snaps at FB.

Ben Sinnott ran 10 routes without being targeted and mainly contributed as a run blocker.

Pressure counts were sourced from PFF.  PFF and PFR use different thresholds for scoring pressures, making their counts not directly comparable, despite being correlated. The higher total pressure counts from PFF provide larger samples for statistical comparisons.

LT Brandon Coleman took the brunt of the Eagles’ pass rush to the tune of 6 pressures in 37 pressure opportunities, including 1 sack. His 13.5% pressure rate is a bottom of the league figure for starting OTs, based on 2025 figures.  His 64.3 run blocking grade was a little below median for OTs. Coleman committed one false start for 5 yards.

RT Josh Conerly fared slightly better, allowing 4 QB hurries in 37 opportunities. His 10.8% pressure rate is a bottom-10% figure based on 2025 numbers.  His 71.5 run block grade was above median for starting OTs. Conerly committed one false start for 5 yards.

LG Chris Paul allowed just 1 pressure in pass protection (pressure rate). His 56.6 run blocking grade was a little below average for a guard.

PFF only credited Nick Allegretti with 1 pressure allowed (2.6% pressure rate), but gave him a substandard 47.3 pass blocking grade.  His 42.1 run blocking grade was the lowest on the Commanders’ OL, and is below standard for a starter.

RG Sam Cosmi was credited with a single pressure in pass protection (2.6% pressure rate).  His 71.6 run blocking grade was the highest on the OL and was above average for starting guards.

DEFENSE

In his debut game with Washington, Defensive Coordinator Daronte Jones delivered on his promise to bring pressure from everywhere. According to PFF, 10 different Commanders pressured Eagles’ QB Jalen Hurts, with the following breakdown by position group:

Interior Defensive Line: 8 pressures, 0 sacks

Off-ball Linebackers: 5 pressures, 2 sacks

Edge Defenders: 4 pressures, 1 sack

Secondary: 1 pressure

Another noteworthy aspect of Jones’ new look defense is that there were no penalties.

Well, that sure is different. Now, let’s see how the individual players fared in the new scheme.

Odafe Oweh recorded 2 TFL, 1 tackle assist, and 1 sack per NFL official stats, for a total of 3 defensive stops.

K’Lavon Chaisson registered just 2 QB hits, per NFL stats. PFR counted 2 missed tackles, while PFF counted 1.  Chaisson dropped into coverage on 6 of 28 passing plays (21.4%). He was targeted twice and allowed 1 reception by WR DeVonta Smith for 10 yds.

Joshua Josephs did not register any official or advanced stats.  But he did throw 325 lb OT Lane Johnson into Jalen Hurts.

It’s a shame that stats aren’t kept on OL bowling. Josephs also dropped into coverage on 1 of 9 pass plays (11.1%) without being targeted.

Javonte Jean-Baptiste did not record any defensive stats.

Daron Payne recorded 1 tackle, for a run stop. According to PFF, he generated 4 QB hurries. His 19.0% pressure rate and 4 total pressures were both the highest on the team. A 19% pressure rate is off the chart, based on 2025 iDL season stats. PFR counted a missed tackle, but PFF did not.

Javon Kinlaw moved around the most of the iDL. He had 1 TFL and 1 tackle assist, both of which contributed to run stops. His 13.3% run stop rate is above the 90th percentile for iDL based on 2025 stats. PFF also recorded 1 QB hurry.

Charles Omenihu had just 1 pass breakup on the official stat sheet.  PFF also recorded 2 QB hurries (14.3% pressure rate). Despite not being designated a starter, Omenihu played the third most defensive snaps on the iDL.

Tim Settle played nose tackle, which is actually a more varied assignment in a Flores-derived scheme than a traditional nose tackle role.  He generated 3 tackle assists, contributing to 1 run stop. His 9.1% run stop rate was above the 90th percentile for iDL based on 2025 season stats. According to PFF, he generated 1 QB hurry in the pass rush. PFF counted 1 missed tackle, which PFR did not see.

Shy Tuttle had 1 tackle assist, which contributed to a run stop. 

Sonny Styles had a productive debut performance in burgundy and gold, splitting snaps between run defense (16), pass rush (8) and coverage (24).  The rookie defender recorded 3 tackles (2 TFL), 1 assist, 1 sack, 1 QB hit, and 3 total defensive stops (2nd on team). PFF counted 2 missed tackles (40% miss rate), while PFR only counted 1 (20%).

In coverage, PFF counted 2 targets and 1 reception by Dallas Goedert for a 43 yd TD.  PFR attributed the reception to another defender.

Frankie Luvu generated 1 TFL, 3 assists, 1 sack and 1 QB hit (2 total stos).  In 15 coverage snaps, PFF recorded 2 targets and 2 receptions for 13 yds.  PFR counted 1 target and reception for 8 yds.

Leo Chenal recorded 1 tackle and 2 assists, with 1 stop. He was not targeted in 12 coverage snaps.  He had 1 missed tackle to spring Saquon Barkley on a long run, and also took teammate Amik Robertson out of the play (25% missed tackle rate). 

Jordan Magee had 1 tackle assist. He generated a QB hurry on 1 blitz and was not targeted in 9 coverage snaps.

Amik Robertson, making his debut for the Commanders, had arguably the best overall defensive performance on the team.  According to PFF, in 35 coverage snaps he was targeted twice, allowing 1 reception for 3 yds (0.09 Y/Cov Snap). Alternatively, PFR counted 3 targets and 2 receptions for 8 yds (0.23 Y/Cov Snap). Either way, is rate of yardage allowed in coverage was in the elite range for a starting CB, indicating either near-total lockdown coverage or other defenders drawing the bulk of the target share.

On the official stat sheet, Robertson recorded 3 tackles and 3 assists, for the second most combined tackles on the team. He recorded 1 defensive stop and 1 missed tackle.

Mike Sainristil played a mixture of boundary and slot corner, with 11 snaps at other alignments. He picked up in coverage where he left off last season, allowing 3 targets and 2 receptions by WR Deontayvion Wicks for 73 yds and 1 TD (2.15 Y/Cov Snap), per PFF.  PFR attributed Wicks’ 64 yd reception to another defender, dropping Sainristil’s yardage total to just 9 yds and a respectable 0.26 Y/Cov Snap.

Sainristil also recorded 4 tackles and 1 assist, with 1 TFL. PFF counted 1 missed tackle, but PFR did not.

Rasul Douglas was targeted 4 times in coverage per PFF (3 tgt per PFR) and allowed 1 reception by WR DeVonta Smith for 39 yds (1.94 Y/Cov Snap).  He made 1 tackle and the only pass breakup by the Commanders’ secondary. PFR counted 1 missed tackle, which PFF did not see.

Making his debut for the Commanders, Bowie MD native Nick Cross recorded 5 tackles, 3 assists and 2 TFL, with 1 missed tackle. He led the team in tackles (5), combined tackles (8) and stops (5). He generated 1 QB hurry in 2 blitz attempts.

Cross mainly split time between free safety, box safety and slot coverage assignments. According to PFF, in 33 coverage snaps, he allowed 3 targets and 3 receptions for 4 yds (0.12 Y/Cov Snp). PFR recorded 5 targets and 4 completions for 47 yds and a TD (1.42 Y/Cov Snap).

Jeremy Reaves played predominantly at free safety and in the box. He recorded 2 tackles and 2 assists. In 35 coverage snaps, PFF recorded 1 target for a 17 yd TD reception by TE Dallas Goedert (0.49 Y/Cov Snap).  PFR recorded 3 targets and 2 rec for 81 yds and the TD (2.31 Y/Cov Snap).

Quan Martin recorded 2 tackles with 1 TFL and 2 total stops.  PFF counted 1 missed tackle, which PFR did not see. In 13 coverage snaps, PFF recorded 2 targets and 2 receptions for 9 receiving yards (0.69 Y/Cov Snap).  PFR recorded 1 target and reception for 12 yds (0.92 Y/Cov Snap). He should play more in Dallas.

SPECIAL TEAMS

Jaylin Lane returned 4 punts for 53 yds with no fair catches or fumbles.  His 13.3 Y/A average ranked 5th in the NFL in Week 1 (min 2 returns). He also returned 3 kickoffs for 95 yds, and a very healthy 31.7 Y/A average.

In his rookie debut, UDFA and Mason/Brennan program graduate Drew Stevens made 1 extra point and had a second attempt blocked by Jalen Carter. Similarly, he made his first field goal attempt from 55 yards in the first quarter, but missed one wide from 54 yards in the third.

Tress Way punted 6 times for a total of 318 yards, with 4 returned for 37 yds (43.5 Net Y/A), 1 touchback and 1 fair caught.  His 9.3 Y/Ret average in the game was more than twice his 2025 season average. 

Rachaad White returned 2 kickoffs for 59 yds (29.5 Y/A).

One day the league will start keeping long snapper stats to allow us to appreciate Tyler Ott’s greatness.

Tyler Owens led the Commanders with 2 coverage tackles, including this one which earned him the coveted Angry Runs Scepter:

Special teams regulars Jordan Magee, Quan Martin, Jeremy Reeves and Javontae Jean-Baptiste each recorded single tackles.

Kain Medrano had 1 tackle and 1 miss.  And Percy Butler just had 1 miss. 

There were no penalties on special teams this week.

item.title: 3 Titans who absolutely need to be better in Week 2
item.description: Identifying three Tennessee Titans players who need to be better versus the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 2.
item.content:encoded:
The Tennessee Titans have a difficult matchup with the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 2. They’ll need to be significantly better than they were versus the New York Jets. We’ve identified three Titans players in particular who need to be way more productive against the Eagles.

Cam Ward, QB

Titans quarterback Cam Ward finished 19-of-32 in Week 1 for 140 yards and a touchdown. A large portion of his production occurred via a garbage-time possession. Ward recorded 55 passing yards and his lone touchdown late in the fourth quarter once the Jets defense went into a late-game prevent shell.

The All-22 tape review wasn’t kind to Ward’s performance. The offensive line was better than the broadcast angles indicated and receivers were creating consistent separation. Ward was hesitant, inefficient, occasionally inaccurate, and even bailed from clean pockets. The sophomore No. 1 overall quarterback needs to get better weekly.

Calvin Ridley, WR

Calvin Ridley doesn’t necessarily need to be “better.” Ward and Brian Daboll need to do a better job getting him involved. The multi-time 1,000-yard receiver wasn’t targeted in Week 1. That’s despite Ridley running 25 routes on 26 passing-down snaps, per Pro Football Focus.

Ridley’s route-participation rate was 96.2%. The aging wideout still possesses enough juice to create explosive plays. Ward and Daboll need to get Ridley involved versus the Eagles to take some pressure off Carnell Tate and Wan’Dale Robinson.

Jermaine Johnson II, EDGE

The Titans traded T’Vondre Sweat to the Jets for Jermaine Johnson II. The former Florida State standout had previously played for Saleh in East Rutherford. That was supposed to make Johnson an effective pass rusher in Saleh’s system, but that wasn’t the case in Week 1.

PFF credited Johnson with registering one pathetic quarterback pressure versus the Jets. The former first-round pick earned a brutal grade of 41.8 as a pass rusher, as he did not impact Geno Smith in the pocket at all. The challenge versus Jalen Hurts will be way bigger.

item.title: Five good Texans questions with Cincy Jungle
item.description: Anthony Cosenza of Cincy Jungle joins BRB for five questions
item.content:encoded:
The Bengals are not as frequent opponent for the Texans as some other teams in the AFC, but whenever they meet you can be sure it is going to be a great game. The recent series has been a little one-sided, but as we saw last week, that guarantees no success for future meetings. The Bengals are always a serious contender with Joe Burrow at the helm. They got off to a great start last week and that is where our conversation got started with Anthony Cosenza of Cincy Jungle.

Battle Red Blog: What did you see in the Bengals week one win that you liked? What concerns came up?

Anthony Cosenza: What the defense showed against a pretty good Buccaneers offense was inspiring. To force four fumbles, collect multiple other pressures and seeing the players swarm to the ball was a sight for sore eyes. It wasn’t a perfect day on that side of the ball, but basically every “new guy” (those brought in over the offseason and/or players who have ascended upwards in roles) had an impact. The offensive line also held up well.

The concerning aspect was on offensive execution. They had to settle for four field goals (including a 56 and 58-yarder), and only won by six points at home while being plus-3 in turnover margin. 

BRB: Who are some new faces that will make a big impact on Sunday?

AC: The interior of the defensive line is making things happen on defense. Dexter Lawrence II and Jonathan Allen are still forces, while rookie Cashius Howell is a spark plug in a rotational role on the edge. Safety Bryan Cook came over from the Chiefs this spring and has steadied the secondary.

On offense, keep an eye out for tight end Erick All Jr. and Dohnte Meyers. All has battled injury, but he provides a skill set for the Bengals to run more under center plays, while Meyers is a great training camp story and is budding as a backend receiver corps gadget player. The former CFL wideout had two touches last week (one catch, one rush), and they both converted big first downs.

BRB: Joe Burrow is consistently one of the top QBs in football. Make your best MVP case for him.

AC: There have already been at least a couple of seasons wherein he could/should have been MVP (he won Comeback Player of the Year in those seasons instead). His leadership is palpable, while his ability to both fit footballs into insanely tight windows and to come back from almost any deficit are some of the best in the game. If the Bengals make the playoffs again, he stays healthy, and puts up stats, he should definitely be on the short list.

BRB: Do you have any key concerns about the Texans offense and defense and how will the Bengals attack that?

AC: Tackling was still a little sloppy on defense (but better), so David Montgomery may be a tough ask. Tampa Bay also exploited the middle part of the field in mid-range passing to Chris Godwin, while Bucky Irving had a number of catches in the flats to net good yardage.

On offense, it’s really about creating more explosive plays, and finishing drives with six points instead of three. Ja’Marr Chase was a non-factor last Sunday, and I don’t expect that to happen again this week, but he does have a tough matchup against the Texans’ secondary.

BRB: Fanduel has the Texans as 2.5 point favorites. How do you see the game going on Sunday? Are there any other bets you feel comfortable recommending?

AC: I think later in the week it has hovered more around three points, but I understand it. Houston is good, and not everyone is sold on the Bengals’ moves and their traditional early season struggles.

This is an extremely tough game, and one wherein I had the Bengals taking one of their only losses towards the beginning of the year. I could see either team winning, but the line feels fair. I’m really interested in the over/under, as it seems low for two teams who combined to score 64 points last week.

We want to thank Anthony for taking the time to answer our questions. Keep in mind that if you want up to the minute news and commentary on the Cincinnati Bengals then you can check out his work on Cincy Jungle. We want to wish Anthony and the Bengals the best of luck for the remainder of the season. As usual, we would like that luck to begin on Monday.

item.title: Ravens DC Anthony Weaver: Tyler Shough reminds me of "a poor-man's Josh Allen"
item.description: Josh Allen's skills were on display in Buffalo's win over the Lions on Thursday night and his performance was the latest reason why any quarterback should be excited about being compared to the Bills star.
item.content:encoded:
Josh Allen's skills were on display in Buffalo's win over the Lions on Thursday night and his performance was the latest reason why any quarterback should be excited about being compared to the Bills star.

That was where Ravens defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver went when he was asked about Saints quarterback Tyler Shough at a Thursday press conference. Weaver said that he believes the "sky's the limit" for the second-year quarterback during an answer that included a comparison to Allen.

"Yes, I like that kid," Weaver said, via a transcript from the team. "We played them towards the latter half of the year when I was in Miami last year, and I was impressed with him then as a rookie. He reminds me a little bit of like a poor-mans Josh Allen. Has all the arm talent in the world [and] can run. I don't think he gets enough credit for how good [of] an athlete he is. So, particularly as you get down to the low red [zone], we are constantly going to be conscious of just his ability to scramble and create those extended plays."

Calling someone a "poor-mans" version of something could be seen as damning with faint praise, but Shough is preparing to make his 11th NFL start so anything that brings Allen to mind is a good sign for where his career can go. A win over the Ravens would be a step toward getting there, but Weaver isn't going to get caught off guard this Sunday.

item.title: 5 Questions with Mile High Report: Broncos Run Defense Is Vulnerable
item.description: Gain intel on the enemy as the Jaguars prepare to face the Broncos in Week 2.
item.content:encoded:
As the Jacksonville Jaguars prepare to face the Denver Broncos in Week 2, we exchanged questions with Ian St. Clair of Mile High Report to learn more about the opposing side.

Question 1: Denver allowed the NFL’s second-most rushing yards last week (220) after allowing the second-fewest rushing yards per game last season (91.1). Are you expecting the defense to bounce back to its 2025 form, or was the 2026 season opener a sign of things to come?

The challenge after the first game of the season is to not let the outcome sway the judgment of a team, one way or the other. It’s one game, and as the cliché goes, one game does not a season make. However, when you look at the last three games for the Broncos’ rush “defense,” it should make Broncos Country cringe. In the last three games, including the two playoff games last season, the Denver defense has allowed 543 yards rushing. That’s a trend, and not a good one. Against a good rushing team in Jacksonville, it may take a miracle for the Broncos to not have this recent nasty streak hit four games. What would help is if the defense remembered how to tackle, though that seems far-fetched at this point, too.

  • Fewer ads

  • Faster commenting and posting experience!

Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android.

Question 2: Bo Nix’s average pass attempt traveled just 4.3 yards in the air in Week 1, which was surprising to see given the offseason addition of Jaylen Waddle. Do you expect the offense to open up more going forward?

This is where I think the anomaly enters the equation. The pairing of opening on the road at Arrowhead Stadium against arguably the best defensive coordinator this century, and an offensive coordinator calling plays in his first game, was a recipe for struggles. Now figure it out and do your job. This isn’t rocket science. You trade for Waddle and he has one catch for two yards. Seriously? Against a secondary that had no returning players to it. On third-and-1, Davis Webb calls an empty set. Seriously? The Broncos offense looked and played like this was its first game playing football. While it’ll take a miracle for the Denver defense to stop the run, Nix and the offense should be much better on Sunday. 

Question 3: Why will this game between Denver and Jacksonville be different than their meeting last season?

Athletes have long memories, and when they’re embarrassed, they’re even longer. Not only did the Jaguars embarrass Denver at home, this team was just unmercifully flogged by Kansas City. Pride is a powerful thing, and the Broncos did make it to the AFC Championship Game with this same roster. The other factor is Sean Payton. He will not accept either type of showing this weekend, and he’ll demand this team figure it out and do its job. Whether that leads to success, we’ll see. The game is also being played in Denver, so that can’t hurt.

Question 4: What’s a key matchup to watch throughout the game?

The Broncos’ front seven against the Jacksonville offensive line. If Denver’s defense doesn’t do a better job of maintaining the edge and fighting off interior blocks on the line of scrimmage, it’ll be a long afternoon. The converse is also true with the Broncos offensive line against the Jacksonville front; run and pass blocking must be better on Sunday than it was in Kansas City.  

Question 5: Do you expect the Broncos to cover as 2.5-point favorites, and do you have a favorite player prop for the game?

This is difficult because, obviously, I’m a Broncos fan. We all witnessed the same thing on Monday night in Kansas City. We also witnessed the same thing last season when these two teams played. But as Nix said after the loss to the Chiefs, this was a “nasty wake-up call.” I think Denver finds a way to cover and get the win on Sunday. As for a prop, I have two: Waddle anytime TD (+185) and 60+ receiving yards (+118).

item.title: Broncos vs Jaguars 5 questions: How does Jacksonville replicate last season’s win?
item.description: The last time these two teams played, the Jags flogged Denver 34-20. Jacksonville will look to replicate that on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
The Denver Broncos have a double dose of motivation this Sunday.

They were embarrassed by the Jacksonville Jaguars the last time these two teams played. The Broncos are coming off a humiliating showing on Monday Night Football in the opener.

Trevor Lawrence and the Jaguars, meanwhile, just whipped Deshaun Watson and the Cleveland Browns. On paper, it looks like Denver is in for another tough afternoon. How does Jacksonville replicate the 34-20 beatdown from last season?

To get a feel for the Jaguars and what they can take from the playoff loss to the Buffalo Bills, we go “behind enemy lines” with Gus Logue from Big Cat Country.

MHR: How tough was the playoff loss to the Bills? What can the Jags take from that loss into this season?

Gus: The loss to Buffalo was brutal. Jacksonville entered last postseason on a league-best eight-game winning streak, highlighted by a convincing dub in Denver. Everyone in Duval County believed they were one of the best teams in the AFC. So the loss was tough because it felt like the Jaguars had a lot more football to play, although they used it as motivation in the offseason. After clobbering the Browns in Week 1, head coach Liam Coen said his team was hungry “to get a bad taste out of their mouth with the first time they played a game since, obviously, Buffalo.” Jacksonville wants to play sticker coverage this season to help its pass rush get home, partly because it couldn’t affect Josh Allen in their Wild Card Round exit.

MHR: Aside from it being against Cleveland, why was Jacksonville so dominant in the opener?

Gus: The top reason was probably the difference in quarterback play. Deshaun Watson’s traditional box score numbers don’t fully reflect how much he tanked Cleveland’s offense with lazy footwork and poor reads. Looking at Expected Points Added, Watson generated -2.8 EPA compared to 18.6 EPA for Trevor Lawrence, who lifted his own offense with aggressive decisions and jaw-dropping touchdowns. Those figures indicate that Jacksonville’s quarterback advantage gave them a 20-point advantage — but the Jags won by 24 — so I would also credit the coaching staff. Coen has proven himself as effective a culture builder as he is a play caller, and you could say the same for defensive coordinator Anthony Campanile, who will become a head coach himself in just a matter of time. The Jaguars have a balanced roster, a franchise quarterback, and a real-deal coaching staff. They were dominant in the season opener because they’re a really good team! It’s not like they won the turnover battle 5-0 or anything.

MHR: How do the Jags replicate last season’s win against the Broncos this Sunday?

Gus: By continuing to lean into a potent passing attack. Lawrence has been letting it rip ever since last season’s Week 10 collapse in Houston, and based on last week’s game, he’s not letting his foot off the pedal. The Jaguars will go under center and use heavy personnel more often this season, but the strength of the team is Lawrence throwing downfield to a receiver room that’s five deep. He’ll pick on cornerbacks not named Surtain in Week 2 the same way he did in last season’s meeting. On the other side of the ball, the Jaguars plan to repeat as the NFL’s No. 1 run defense, so they’ll key in on J.K. Dobbins and screen plays to make Bo Nix beat them with his arm. Campanile only blitzed Nix on 14.3% of dropbacks in their last meeting, which was the second-lowest rate for the Jaguars all season, but he may want to turn up the dial after seeing Nix take 4 sacks against the Chiefs in Week 1.

MHR: What are your thoughts on the current spread? And what is your best bet for Sunday’s game?

Gus: It’s tempting to take the points with the Jaguars. They beat the Broncos by two touchdowns last season, and since that game, I’ve grown more confident in Jacksonville and less confident in Denver. I still view the Broncos as Super Bowl contenders because their depth chart and coaching staff are too good to ignore — but IDK about Bo, y’all. As for my best bet for Sunday, I like Parker Washington to go over 51.5 receiving yards. He had a career-high 145 yards against the Broncos last year and a game-high 83 yards against the Browns last week. He’s the No. 1 pass-catcher on what projects to be a top-10, maybe even top-5 passing offense. His weekly receiving yard props should be in the 70s or 80s soon.

MHR: What are your expectations and predictions for Sunday?

Gus: I don’t want to fall victim to recency bias, but it was hard to watch Monday Night Football and not get excited about what Jacksonville’s under-center run game could do against Denver. Second-year running back Bhayshul Tuten looked impressive in the season opener. According to PFF, the only player with more broken tackles last week was … wait for it … Kenneth Walker III. I’ll predict a breakout game for Tuten and a second-half interception by Travis Hunter to seal another double-digit-point win at Mile High. Jaguars 23, Broncos 13.

item.title: Week 2 Prediction: New Orleans Saints vs. Baltimore Ravens
item.description: Week 2 finds the Saints on the road again, this time in Baltimore
item.content:encoded:
The New Orleans Saints came painfully close to pulling off a Week 1 upset. Now, the challenge doesn’t get any easier.

New Orleans will remain on the road Sunday when it travels to Baltimore to face the Ravens in M&T Bank Stadium, as they look to bounce back from a heartbreaking 31-30 overtime loss to the Detroit Lions.

Despite the loss, there were plenty of positives for the Saints.

After falling behind 21-0, they battled all the way back to force overtime and nearly escaped Ford Field with a victory. Quarterback Tyler Shough delivered an impressive performance, throwing for 410 yards and three touchdowns despite committing three turnovers. Chris Olave was his favorite target, hauling in 10 passes for 182 yards.

If nothing else, the comeback showed this Saints team is very capable of responding when things go wrong.

But they can’t afford another slow start against Baltimore.

The Ravens opened their season with a dominant 41-23 victory over the Indianapolis Colts, piling up 506 yards of total offense. Lamar Jackson threw for 324 yards, while Derrick Henry rushed for 144 yards and three touchdowns.

That combination presents a major challenge for a New Orleans defense that struggled early against Detroit before settling in as the game progressed. Containing Jackson is difficult enough, but the Saints will also have to find a way to slow Henry down and keep Baltimore from controlling the game on the ground.

There is, however, some uncertainty surrounding the Ravens’ offense. Wide receiver Zay Flowers, who had 150 receiving yards in Week 1, left the game with a hamstring injury, so his status ????

For New Orleans, the biggest question may be whether Tyler Shough can build on his Week 1 performance while eliminating the costly mistakes.

Throwing for over 4o0 yards in his first start of the season was impressive, especially after the Saints fell into such a large early hole. But three turnovers against a team as talented as Baltimore could quickly put New Orleans in another situation where it is forced to play from behind.

The Saints showed enough in Detroit to make me believe they can keep this game competitive. Shough and Olave showed they can create explosive plays, and the team displayed the kind of resilience that had been missing for a while.

Still, Baltimore presents an even tougher challenge.

Playing Jackson and Henry on the road is a difficult assignment for any defense, and unless the Saints can force Baltimore into some mistakes of its own, I think the Ravens ultimately make enough plays late to remain undefeated.

Prediction: Ravens 31 – Saints 27

New Orleans may leave Baltimore 0-2, but if Shough can clean up the turnovers and the Saints once again go toe-to-toe with one of the NFL’s better teams on the road, there will still be plenty of reason to believe this team is heading in the right direction.

item.title: Patriots need ‘competitive stamina’ on point in battle with T.J. Watt
item.description: The reigning AFC Defensive Player of the Week is coming to town in Week 2.
item.content:encoded:
Coming out of the Pittsburgh Steelers’ season opener, T.J. Watt added yet another accolade to his Hall of Fame résumé. For a ninth time in his career, the standout edge rusher was named the AFC’s Defensive Player of the Week.

He was effectively guaranteed the award the moment he left Pittsburgh’s Acrisure Stadium field last Sunday. Watt notched two sacks in his team’s 20-13 win over the Atlanta Falcons, and scored the decisive points when he returned an interception 35 yards for his first career pick-six.

Long story short, the 31-year-old is not showing any signs of slowing down. For the New England Patriots, that very well could be a problem.

Entering their Week 2 matchup with the Steelers in an 0-1 hole, the Patriots are under pressure already to earn a victory against a team likely to also battle for a playoff spot in the AFC. Earning that win starts with not letting Watt dictate the game like he did versus the Falcons.

The question is how to do that. For Patriots offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels, one key ingredient is fighting fire with fire: matching the intensity he is guaranteed to bring to the table.

“It’s difficult to play harder than him,” McDaniels told the media on Thursday. “I think it’s probably one of the greatest compliments a coach could give to an opposing player, just the effort and the competitive nature that he demonstrates on literally every play. And so, when you line up against him, whether you’re the tight end, tackle, whoever it is — and he’ll be on both sides of the ball — you have to do a great job of having great competitive stamina. Because that’s what he’s going to play with.

“And the minute you let up, he always seems to capitalize. There are not many players that get as much attention as he does, in terms of the offense trying to limit his production and his impact. The consistency with which he comes through with big plays, week after week, year after year, even though that’s happening is pretty amazing.”

Against the Falcons last week, Watt lined up in his usual spot on the defensive left edge on 32 of 38 defensive snaps. The task of matching his competitive stamina on Sunday will therefore primarily fall on veteran Morgan Moses, a player well-familiar with the six-time All-Pro.

Last year, Moses and Watt lined up opposite one another 60 times. The Patriots wisely shied away from exclusively trying their luck in 1-on-1 combat, using a variety of blocking structures to limit his impact. And even so, he finished the game with four quarterback pressures, including two sacks. He also forced a fumble and recovered one to help set up Pittsburgh’s game-winning drive.

Unsurprisingly, Moses knows the challenge that awaits.

“The same T.J. Watt. He never changes,” he said. “Consistent, knack for the ball, great pass rusher. He’s going to play every down full speed. That’s what you get from him.”

Moses was beaten for one of Watt’s sacks the last time they faced off in Week 3 of the 2025 season. For him, this latest battle against the star defender will be more than a physical one, however. He knows his mental game also needs to be on point.

“It’s a mental appointment,” he explained. “You know what he is, you know what he stands for. He’s been the face of that team for a long time. And so, anytime you have a guy who not just fills the stat sheet on sacks but PBUs, interceptions, forced fumbles, the things that he does that create turnovers for that team, you have to be able to obviously block him to the whistle and be ready for that challenge.”

item.title: Digging into the numbers to predict Cowboys vs Commanders
item.description: Comparing the numbers from week 1 for Dallas and Washington
item.content:encoded:
Every week, we’ll examine the numbers behind the next opponent on the schedule. We’ll look at historical data points as well as more recent numbers. At the end, we’ll add it all up to see what Dallas needs to do to secure a win and which team may have the edge.

The history

The Cowboys lead the Commanders in head-to-head matchup all-time 81-49-2.

The Dak Prescott-led Cowboys are 13-2 against the Commanders. In five of those wins, Dak was pulled out early with the game locked up well before the end of the fourth quarter.

In 15 games, Dak Prescott has thrown for 3,716 yards, 32 touchdowns, five interceptions, and has a passer rating of 107.4. This is his best passer rating against any team in the NFC East.

The most thrilling matchup between the two teams came in week 12 of 2024. This game featured seven scores in just the fourth quarter alone, including an electric kick return touchdown from KaVontae Turpin.

Bounce back game?

The Cowboys have not started 0-2 since 2010.

Dak Prescott is 5-0 in the games immediately following a week one loss.

Nearly 90% of teams that start 0-2 go on to miss the playoffs. In 2025, every team that started the season with two losses missed the playoffs.

Cowboys key stats from last week

Prescott threw for 175 yards, two touchdowns, and one interception.

The longest play on offense for the Cowboys went for just 17 yards.

The defense allowed a 134.2 passer rating from Jaxson Dart, gave up 165 yards on the ground, and allowed the Giants to chew up enormous amounts of clock on their way to the endzone throughout the game.

Commanders key stats from last week

Jayden Daniels threw for 164 yards against the Eagles and added another 31 yards on the ground.

Philadelphia was able to pressure Daniels on 19 of 38 drop backs, resulting in the quarterback going 3-15 for 26 yards through the air.

Against the blitz, Daniels went 5-7 for 47 yards and two touchdowns against Philadelphia’s blitz.

The Commanders defense gave up explosive plays of 64, 43, 42, 41, 22 yards against the Eagles. They had a difficult time covering Dallas Goedert who had four receptions for 77 yards and two touchdowns.

What do the numbers mean?

The numbers lied to us last week. There were too many unknowns with the entirely new system and coaching staff in New York. This week tells us a clearer story.

The Commanders’ defense forced five three-and-outs and seven Philadelphia punts. 138 of Jalen Hurts’ 203 passing yards came on just three plays. Of Saquon Barkley’s 83 rushing yards, 42 came on one rushing attempt. The Commanders are susceptible to big plays, but without those chunks, their defense was stout against the Eagles. It will be important for Dallas to utilize their weapons on the outside early and often to generate those big plays.

After last week, the Cowboys should decide it’s time to start the game by airing the ball out. Before the season started, Sharp Football had the Commanders’ secondary ranked 31st in the league, and last week’s tape confirmed it. Dallas should target Mike Sainristil as much as possible with CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens as he was the weakest link in week one, giving up over 35 yards per reception.

If Dallas takes the route of attacking the Commanders’ defensive backfield with chunk plays, it’ll be important for the offensive line to hold up against a solid pass rush consisting of Odafe Oweh, Dorance Armstrong, K’Lavon Chaisson and Daron Payne. Dallas will also need to look out for a blitzing Sonny Styles, who absolutely crushed Saquon Barkley on his way to a Jalen Hurts sack last week.

On the other side of the ball, this defense will be looking to redeem themselves after a poor week one outing against the Giants. One key piece of information to keep in mind this week: blitzing Jayden Daniels may not be the best idea. Last week, Daniels struggled when the Eagles forced pressure without sending an extra man, completing just three out of fifteen attempts for 26 yards. However, when they attacked the pocket with the blitz, Daniels threw for two touchdowns and had a completion percentage of 71.4%.

This week, getting home without sending extra blitzers will be one of the most important keys to the game. If this defense can do that in addition to fixing their mental mistakes from week one, they’ll find themselves back on track.

Given the history of the Cowboys’ ability to avoid 0-2, and a massive strength on weakness matchup between Dallas’ receivers/Washington’s defensive backs, a bounce-back game is the reasonable expectation in week two. It would be surprising to see the Dallas offense struggle to launch again this week. 27 or more points feels like a lock against the Commanders.

The real question will be how often the Cowboys defense can give the ball back to this offense. All things considered, the odds favor Dallas at home this week with a win against their division rival.

item.title: Miami Dolphins reasons for hope, concern heading into Week 2
item.description: There is hope for the Dolphins this week. Or maybe not.
item.content:encoded:
Howdy y’all.  I’m a little behind this week, so I didn’t get to watch and write all the stuff I wanted to for here or AOR.  I’m trying to develop a few regular posts for this site each week to keep all y’all as engaged as possible.  You know, given what this season is and all.  Y’all saw the Tuesday Thoughts post, and I’m gonna make that one a regular.  If y’all have any ideas for additional posts, let me know.

Anyway… I figured I would start a post with 3 things to watch for in each game that promote optimism and 3 things that should make us worried.  Aside from the usual stuff.  So welcome to The Earl’s Three For Three!

Three Reasons for Hope

1. Experience Has Been Gained

Last week, the Dolphins’ rookies played 27.2% of the possible snaps.  That was league-leading and nearly 10% more than the next closest team (Browns at 16.7%).  Over a quarter of the snaps were played by someone who had never taken an NFL snap.  Chris Johnson, Jacob Rodriguez, and Kadyn Proctor played every snap.  Caleb Douglas, Michael Taaffe, and Chris Bell played 91%, 75%, and 52%, respectively.  Not all of this was pretty.  Johnson was picked on early and often, and Taaffe missed a few assignments.  But this week, they know what it’s like.  They know the feeling of stepping onto an NFL field for the first time.  Once upon a time, I had the opportunity to interview Cameron Wake over the phone for The Phinsider.  I asked him about his first experience in the NFL, and he talked about that feeling when you first step out there and think, “I made it.”  I imagine it was overwhelming for these young players, even ones like Proctor who played for one of the biggest college programs out there.  But not only is the first-time feeling gone, but they also have a good idea of what the play is like at the NFL level.  I recall a comment from Hall of Fame LB Patrick Willis about getting hit by Edgerrin James in his first game and realizing what “grown man” strength was and how the NFL is on a different level. That’s gone now.  These rookies have seen the real game now. They have felt the real game now.  They still don’t know enough yet, but they won’t be as surprised now.  That’ll lead to smarter and quicker decisions, better communication, and higher confidence.

2. There Is Hope Up Front

The Rams are a true Super Bowl contender, and the 49ers shut them down.  That should be scary, right?  Not necessarily.  Despite the outcome, the Rams still put up 290 yards of offense, with 122coming on the ground.  The 49ers allowed the Rams a 4.2 YPC average.  There was also not a single sack in this game.  The 49ers generated 8 pressures on 29 dropbacks, but recorded no sacks.  Miami’s offensive line isn’t as accomplished as LA’s, but they should have extra motivation this week after how they performed against Vegas.  The 49ers can’t just pin their ears back and rush the passer either.  Matthew Stafford is great at maneuvering the pocket, but he does not have the ability to threaten defenses on the ground like Malik Willis.  They may play more “contain” rather than straight rush.  All it takes is for him or Achane to hit a big play to force the defense to play honest.  This is a chance for the offensive line to make a statement against a front that is not quite as formidable.

3. Caleb Douglas Is A Weapon

The most important thing Douglas has brought to the Dolphins is his ability to get open.  Much has been made about his size and speed since the draft.  His stat line stood out and set franchise records.  But what really stood out in week one was his ability to create separation.  Douglas generated 5.3 yards of separation at the catch, despite having less cushion than other receivers.  The Raiders tried to press him, and he still won.  Of course, the Raiders secondary isn’t exactly loaded with premier talent.  But for a rookie in his first game, and on the road, he stood out in a big way.  He’ll have a much tougher test this week.  The 49ers’ defensive back group, led by emerging star Renardo Green, is more talented than Las Vegas’s.  Now that word is out on Douglas, he will get far more attention.  But nothing suggests Douglas will fail to succeed this week. He is quickly becoming a go-to weapon and potentially a star.

Three Areas of Concern

1. The 49ers Are Also Strong Up Front

The Rams gained 122 yards on the ground, which is nice.  But the 49ers gained 174 yards on the ground.  And did so with only 1 more attempt than the Rams.  They leaned heavily on both CMC and rookie Kaelon Black, with CMC going 10-68 and Black going 14-65.  Deebo Samuel got in on the act with a 12-yard carry. The Niners did not record a single negative run play.  This is a frightening idea, as the Dolphins were just pantsed by Ashton Jeanty and the Raiders, who, while talented, only had a 3.7 YPC average last season and an offensive line as maligned as the Dolphins’.  The Dolphins will need to tighten up SIGNIFICANTLY if they want to have any hope of containing the 49ers rushing attack.  The Niners’ passing game wasn’t necessarily special.  Purdy went 25-for-34 for 205 yards.  That’s a YPA of 6.1, which is meh.  But he also threw 3 TDs.  He was also not under any pressure whatsoever, despite the Rams having added the reigning defensive player of the year in Myles Garrett.  Garrett is now on IR, but he played 40 snaps and generated 1 pressure.  As a team, the Rams generated three total pressures.  Miami generated 4 pressures last week.  Granted, the Dolphins didn’t earn the right to rush the passer, and Cousins got the ball out quickly.  Purdy also had time to throw quickly.  Regardless, the Dolphins failed the test against a Raider front and now face a much better offensive line.

2. Kyle Shanahan Is A Madman

If you read my most recent article at Aqua And Orange Review, I highlighted some offensive personnel and defensive package tendencies from the first week of action.  The Niners defense was mostly base 4-3 until they got a big enough lead to force LA to throw more.  Miami was heavily 11-personnel, which may have been due to their situation.  The flip side to this is that Kyle Shanahan does not stick to any one personnel grouping exclusively.  I’ll let you read the AOR article for that, but his ability to use a variety of groupings for any play call will keep Miami’s young and inexperienced defense on their heels.  Jeff Hafley has his tendencies too, but whether he can go toe-to-toe with Shanahan is a big question, especially with this group.  They have worked together, so they know each other well.  It may come down to the talent more than the Xs & Os.  I think Hafley will have some answers, but this defense hasn’t seen the funkShanahan is about to throw at them.

3. Miami’s Linebackers Are Good; San Francisco’s Linebackers Are Better

I thought about discussing the plethora of playmakers at the 49ers’ disposal and how it will be a “pick your poison” situation for the defense.  I thought about discussing some of Brock Purdy’s playmaking skills.  But those are obvious choices that everyone discusses.  I want to look at another position group: the linebackers.  Jordyn Brooks is an All-Pro, and Jacob Rodriguez looked good in his first action for the Dolphins.  But the 49ers have the best LB in the game with Fred Warner and a solid running mate in Dre Greenlaw.  They will close the middle of the field for the Dolphins.  They will allow the 49ers to call coverages that some teams could not call due to LB limitations.  This will force the Dolphins to call plays that avoid where Warner and Greenlaw are camping out.  Even if they are out of position or away from the play, they have the range to get in on the action.  This also affects the run game and the intermediate passing game.  Slowik will have to get creative to neutralize those players.  Miami hopes to have a linebacking duo that becomes one of the best in the league.  This week, they face the prototype.

I said what I said

Three areas of hope.  Three areas of concern.  What more can you ask for?  I’m not going to sugar coat the situation: the Dolphins are outgunned and outclassed in every aspect of this contest.  The 49ers have weapons upon weapons on both sides of the ball.  The Dolphins… don’t.  Maybe in a couple of years, this youth movement will pay dividends, and a rebuilding team looks at Miami as outclassing them.  But I can’t see much hope for a win here.  Maybe everything clicks at the same time, but it will probably be ugly.  Still, if Miami can get some contributions from the young’uns and show some growth from week one, that’s a win for this team.

item.title: NFL Survivor contest picks, predictions, advice, strategy: My favorite Week 2 selections
item.description: NFL Survivor pools are back and Matt Russell runs through Week 2, giving his favorite picks to help you advance.
item.content:encoded:
For weeks leading up to Week 1, the Pittsburgh Steelers looked like they might be the slick play in Survivor contests, as a 3.5-point favorite over the Falcons. Then, on Thursday of last week, Tua Tagovailoa went down with an oblique injury in practice, and it was like someone jumped on a bullhorn and said, "Hey! Look over here!" Both the point spread and Pittsburgh's usage in Survivor contests went up.  

We'll never know what would have happened if Tagovailoa had played on Sunday, but the Steelers definitely took advantage of a start by Cooper Rush, using a defensive touchdown to stretch an otherwise precarious lead.

The Jaguars didn't need any high-leverage plays as they were the rocking-chair winner of the week, while the Chargers wiped out a whopping 32.5% of entrants on Yahoo Survival Football.

Each week (until we've exhausted all reasonable paths of survival), we'll look at the Survivor Contest landscape, and the best options available, while understanding that it matters who you've already taken, and what you might be giving up by burning a team that week.

Week 2 moneylines

How likely is a team to win and you'll advance? The betting market provides the answer to that each week with the moneyline, which we can convert to an implied win probability.

Market power ratings

It's not as simple as picking the team most likely to win, because once you use that team, you can't use it again. What is simple is that if you're going to make it through the 18-week season, then you need to use 18 teams. That means, at some point, you'll be trusting the 18th-best team in the NFL — an unnerving thought. 

Here's a list of the current top 18 teams (with help from the betting market), and an estimation of their value to the point spread: 

  • Rams: 18.9

  • Bills: 18.6

  • Ravens: 18.6

  • 49ers: 17.6

  • Chiefs: 17.0

  • Bears: 16.7

  • Texans: 16.5

  • Eagles: 16.2

  • Patriots: 16.2

  • Lions: 15.9

  • Broncos: 15.7

  • Bengals: 15.4

  • Chargers: 15.1

  • Cowboys: 14.9

  • Jaguars: 14.9

  • Seahawks: 14.6

  • Packers: 14.0

  • Buccaneers: 13.8

Picking the most likely team to win each week, or the highest available team on this list above, means that you're giving up the opportunity to use it later, and while every week is technically created equal, trusting a team in September is nerve-wracking, but doing so at some point in December is real tension. 

Week 2's top choices

As we look at the best options for Week 1 and onward, we'll be factoring in the decision tree that will sprout from that pick. The implied probability derived from the moneyline should answer any questions about why the favorite should win, but the nuance is found in what you're giving up by using it now and not later (with a projected point spread projection for those matchups). 

49ers (87.6%) over Dolphins 

The Dolphins couldn't give the Raiders much of a contest in Week 1, so why would you expect Miami to shock the 49ers? 

It depends on what you believe the after-effects might be of the 49ers' trip to Australia. While the Rams looked to be the jet-lagged team on the field in Week 1, spending more time Down Under might create lingering issues for San Francisco. 

The betting market downgraded the Fins to the worst team in the league already, while also moving the relatively healthy Niners up among the highest power-rated teams. 

Estimated availability: 100%

What you're giving up (projected point spread):

  • Week 3 vs Cardinals (SF -8.5)

  • Week 9 vs. Raiders (SF -9.5)

There won't be many two-touchdown favorites all season. At least, not until quarterback injuries start to submarine some teams' seasons, so, this should be the biggest favorite the Niners will be all season. Plus, while San Francisco might be a 10-point favorite against the Cardinals next week, we've already seen Arizona do some damage in Survivor contests. 

Saving the Niners for next week, only to see the Cardinals potentially beat the Seahawks this week would up the anxiety in fading Arizona. That said, a peak at lookahead lines suggests there might be just three games with a spread over a touchdown in Week 3.

If you're saving the 49ers for Week 9, you're hoping their key players are still healthy, and you might also hope the Raiders have turned to rookie Fernando Mendoza by then.

Buccaneers (78.6%) over Browns 

Call me crazy, but I like to take a (good) team off a loss in Survivor contests. You know you'll get the best effort out of them. 

Tampa Bay didn't punt in Week 1. It also didn't come all that close to beating the Bengals, as too many of their possessions ended on fumbles, and Joe Burrow made the Bucs pay. 

Deshaun Watson continued to show no inclination that he and the Browns would do anything with extra possessions, if they were given them. Nor did Cleveland's defense provide any resistance in Jacksonville either. 

Estimated availability: 100%

What you're giving up (projected point spread):

  • Week 8 vs. ATL (TB -7.5)

The Buccaneers barely crack our top-18 teams in the NFL, and our projected spread for the only other conceptual time where they would be a viable option is using the Falcons' current betting market power-rating number — one fraught with quarterback issues. However, by Week 8, with Michael Penix Jr. potentially healthy, Atlanta's rating will be higher, and the projected point spread considerably tighter. Essentially, it may be now or never to use the Bucs.

Eagles (74.9%) over Titans 

As noted above, there are plenty of teams with a 70% win probability, but Survivor is about both strategy and elements of game handicapping. We're including the Eagles here, not because we want to use the lone road team in that cohort this week, but more as a representative of the others priced in a similar way. 

The Rams have the same latent jet lag issues as the 49ers, but with a more game opponent in the Giants. The Chargers just burned nearly a third of Survivor entrants, and we can't be sure the Raiders are worse than the Cardinals. The Chiefs are coming off a short week, where they were able to win thanks to simply handing the ball to Kenneth Walker and watching him break the Broncos' missed tackles, but more may be required to beat the Colts.

The Eagles offense was hit-and-miss at home against the Commanders with almost half of their total yards coming on three plays, but that should be enough to beat the Titans, who are still dreadful.

Estimated availability: 96.9%

What you're giving up (projected point spread):

  • Week 7 vs. Panthers (PHI -6)

  • Week 10 vs. Giants (PHI -5.5)

The difference between playing at home versus on the road is evident here, given the next-best times to pick the Eagles come against more capable teams, at home, with a spread around a touchdown as well. 

By comparison, the other team with a 70% win probability that we haven't referenced — the Ravens, still have the Titans early in the season (Week 4) and the Browns at home late (Week 16). 

In the end, Week 2 provides a pair of strong options in the 49ers and Buccaneers that are both high-probability favorites and teams you may not miss out on using later in the season.

item.title: The Packers will look to repeat some history from 2014 (well, mostly)
item.description: A comeback win against the Jets in week 2 that season got the Packers back on track. Is it time to repeat history?
item.content:encoded:
In 2014, the Green Bay Packers started off the season with an embarrassing defeat on the road. They went into Seattle and got throttled by the Seahawks, losing 36-16 in a game that didn’t even really feel that close. Panic set in among the fan base, and the season felt over when it had barely begun.

Of course, week one can lie. The very next week, the Packers played the New York Jets, quarterbacked by a young Geno Smith, and got their season back on track. It took a bit — the Jets jumped out to a shocking 21-3 lead in the second quarter — but Green Bay closed the gap in the second and third quarters, getting two touchdowns from Randall Cobb and a big 80-yarder from Jordy Nelson to provide the game-winning score in a 31-24 victory.

It was the kind of response to adversity that the 2026 Packers need to channel this week when the team, coming off an embarrassing road loss in week one, plays a New York Jets squad quarterbacked by a much older Geno Smith. The parallels are all there for the taking. The Packers just need to go out and make it happen. (Preferably, without the drama of getting out to a big early deficit.)

Here’s a combination of some looks ahead to this week 2 matchup as well as a few last postmortems of the week 1 debacle in Minnesota.

3 things on Packers offense vs Jets: Can O-line rebound vs the blitz? | Packers Wire
The Jets won’t blitz as often as the Vikings did — nobody did and nobody can — but they’re still one of the more blitz-happy defenses in the NFL. It’s on the coaching staff and the players to fix the communication issues that plagued the line last Sunday.

item.title: Sean McVay hopeful Rams don’t play in Australia again
item.description: Sean McVay may never want to go to Australia again and more NFL type news on a Friday!
item.content:encoded:
If teleportation existed, and or had the Los Angeles Rams won in Australia, then perhaps Sean McVay would feel different, but as it stands McVay is happy the game in Australia is over. McVay is hopeful the Rams never have to play a game like that again.

McVay, a true company man, says the atmosphere down under was “great”, however one can assume the travel, the idea of playing so far from home, the fact that L.A. got whooped up on, McVay appears content to leave that game and experience in the past.

It’s interesting, and maybe one day we’ll hear McVay talk about what went right and what went wrong during the team’s preparation for their Australian game. As it stands, what we know is the Rams lost, and now they want to turn the page. Easier said than done.

From the sound of it, Week 1 isn’t exactly all in the past, yet. In fact, Week 1 is still very much in the present, until the Rams can give fans a reason to believe otherwise. If winning is a cure-all, then losing is a deadly poison. The Rams are 0-2 in their last two games played. Facts. Can they find a cure Monday night?

Tune in, find out.

Sean McVay hopes Rams never play again in Australia; Aaron Donald’s status undecided (latimes.com)

“McVay said the Rams have moved forward from the loss to the 49ers.

“It’s almost like you try and do the ‘Men in Black’ thing,” McVay said, referencing the movie franchise, “where you say all right, ‘hey I don’t remember what happened.’ That was so long ago. We’re not playing in Australia ever again, I hope. Not because it wasn’t a great atmosphere. That will get taken out of context.”

Sean McVay hopes the Rams never play in Australia again (nbcsports)

“Bottom line is, I like the way that I feel of our preparation, eyes moving forward, chest out, chin up, eyes forward, and let’s go be about it,” McVay said. “Let’s go prepare the right way. Let’s have great focus and concentration. Let’s have a great energy and an edge in which we prepare and compete with and then let’s go be ready to go against a really damn good football team. What they looked like in Week 1, we got a great challenge ahead. That’s what every week is. We’re excited to compete. All we can do is really have a great day of preparation today.”

Curl, Speights and Landman were all listed as limited participants on Thursday, while Kinchens missed practice altogether. Davante Adams got a veteran rest day, too.“

Rams, Packers, Chargers, Patriots: Which Week 1 losses should scare us most? (cbssports)

“Super Bowl odds. That gave us 53 historical losses to compare with what happened over the rest of the season.

The biggest takeaway might also be the most reassuring: If your team was supposed to be good before Week 1, getting blown out wasn’t much worse than a close loss. What mattered much more was how the team played.

The good news: If a contender got blown out, the blowout itself isn’t the problem

A Week 1 loss matters. Preseason contenders that won their opener from 2015-2025 made the playoffs 73% of the time, while those that lost fell to 42%. But once a contender lost, the margin barely mattered — one-score losers made the playoffs 41% of the time, and teams beaten by nine or more made it roughly 43% of the time.“

What Sean McVay said about potential Aaron Donald return for Rams against Giants (clutchpoints)

It will be up to Donald, the Rams coaching staff and the team’s medical personnel to decide if the Monday night game is the right time for him to return, according to McVay.

The Rams were decisive favorites to supplant the Seattle Seahawks in the NFC West and go on to win the Super Bowl prior to the start of the season. While the Rams played poorly in their trip Down Under, there’s no reason for McVay or his team to panic.“

item.title: Chiefs expect the Colts to rebound from disappointing Week 1
item.description: Despite coming off of a blowout loss, Kansas City sees a dangerous team in Indianapolis.
item.content:encoded:
Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season could not have gone more differently for the Kansas City Chiefs and the Indianapolis Colts. The two teams face off in Week 2’s edition of “Sunday Night Football.”

The day before, the Chiefs delivered a dominant 31-10 victory over the Denver Broncos on “Monday Night Football,” while the Colts surrendered over 500 yards of offense in a 41-23 loss to the Baltimore Ravens.

For their part, the Colts gained only 251 total yards while surrendering two turnovers and two sacks.

Even after a showcase performance by his own unit against Denver, Chiefs defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo does not expect the Colts’ first game to reflect what they can bring.

Any time he prepares for the Colts, Spagnuolo is wary of star running back Jonathan Taylor, who gained 121 yards from scrimmage and scored two touchdowns against Baltimore.

“He’s really good,” Spagnuolo observed before Thursday’s practice. “One thing we have to do is try to bottle him up. When he gets to the edge…he’s really good. If you remember from the game a year ago, it was a short-yardage play that he popped. He’s tough to catch, so trying to get him bottled up and not let him hit a seam north and south would be really good.”

Colts quarterback Daniel Jones was middling in his first game back from an Achilles tear late last season. Spagnuolo expects better from the veteran.

“We can’t be deceived by this quarterback, thinking he’s a statue,” the coach remarked. “He’s a really good athlete, too. And they have option football in their game; their coaches do a really good job of it.”

Spagnuolo believes Jones makes Taylor a more dangerous back.

“When Daniel Jones and Taylor are playing together,” he explained, “Taylor plays really well because you have the threat of the quarterback throwing it, so they’re dual threat in that regard… I’m not deceived by the fact that they didn’t have a great game last week.”

The Chiefs also expect the Indianapolis defense’s veterans to rebound after an embarrassing opening week. Their defensive coordinator, Lou Anarumo, also has a long track record of finding creative formations to thwart the Chiefs’ offense.

“If you look at their defensive line, their safeties, their corners,” noted quarterback Patrick Mahomes on Wednesday, “they have really good football players or linebackers. So, they’ll have a lot of pride, and they’ll come out with the right mentality. They won a lot of football games last year off their defense, and Coach Anarumo is one of the best defensive coordinators I’ve went up against.”

item.title: Browns Week 2: Scouting Baker Mayfield, the Tampa Bay Buccaneers
item.description: In Week 2, the Cleveland Browns and Tampa Bay Bucs will face off. What will the home team, Baker Mayfield bring?
item.content:encoded:
As the Cleveland Browns look to reset after a lackluster season opener, the team returns to Florida to visit old friend quarterback Baker Mayfield and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers this Sunday. After making the playoffs in 2024, the Buccaneers missed the postseason last season in a favorable NFC South. On paper, Tampa’s team looks different than last year’s, but some might argue the team is better than they were last season.

It’s an argument that some can make, but last Sunday in their loss against the Cincinnati Bengals, the team has some questions that need to be answered.

Baker Mayfield gets paid… then…

Quarterback Baker Mayfield went through a contract dispute throughout the offseason with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers until it was eventually settled and he was able to get a new deal.

As far as how Mayfield looked on Sunday, it was why Tampa was hesitant to give him max money. Despite not throwing any interceptions, Mayfield fumbled the ball three times and lost all three. Whether it was Mayfield looking ahead to this game (for reasons that are personal), despite the good moments, he had the lack of ball security really put the Buccaneers behind the 8-ball.

It would be disingenuous to say that this game isn’t personal for Mayfield. In his eyes, the Cleveland Browns essentially gave up on him. The reality is the Browns wanted to upgrade at the quarterback position; Mayfield was upset and reacted immaturely, and the team replaced him with the person who fans want the team to get rid of.

In Week 1, Tampa’s quarterback was both the reason they were in the game and the reason they ended up losing. Which Mayfield will Cleveland’s defense see on Sunday?

How good are the Bucs?

After re-watching the Bucs-Bengals All-22, it’s fair to say that this team could’ve won against the Bengals. If Mayfield didn’t turn the ball over as much as he did, the team could’ve won. The receiver room looks different as wide receiver Mike Evans is now in the Bay Area with the San Francisco 49ers. Wide receiver Emeka Egbuka is the top WR on the team, and veteran Chris Godwin is the reliable veteran in the room. On the offensive line, Tristan Wirfs is one of the best tackles in the league.

Defensively, the unit looks different but should be improved. Rookie Reuben Bain Jr. was considered the top defensive end in his draft class, and rookie Josiah Trotter seems to be a future Pro Bowler. Overall, this team is talented, but it’s hard to say if this team is better than the Jacksonville Jaguars.

Is head coach Todd Bowles coaching for his job?

It’s a fair question to ask. Bowles has been with the Buccaneers for a long time, and the team has routinely been a playoff team with him at the helm. However, last season the team stumbled down the stretch and showed cracks in the foundation that Bowles has maintained. It’s fair to say that Tampa Bay has plateaued with Bowles. Good team in a weak division but hasn’t shown the ability to make a deep playoff run. The Bucs haven’t advanced past the divisional round since the year they won the Super Bowl. If the Buccaneers miss the postseason again or face an early exit, it’s fair to say that the Buccaneers will be searching for a new head coach in 2027.
