item.content:encoded:
Earlier this year, there was a lot of talk about the future of Buffalo Bills wide receiver Keon Coleman. He was suspended a few times in 2025 for being late to team meetings, and even Bills owner Terry Pegula had less than flattering things to say about him. But new head coach Joe Brady and QB Josh Allen said in February that they believed in him and when it came time to step up against the Detroit Lions, he did just that.

Coleman caught six passes on six targets for 63 yards despite playing out of position for a good chunk of the game filling in for DJ Moore. Moore was injured in the first half of the game, and Buffalo didn’t have another speedy receiver. Coleman has faced his problems and spoke to the media when he didn’t have to. He’s taken accountability. On Thursday night he stepped up in a big way when the Bills needed him. With Moore likely to miss time with his injury, they’ll need Coleman more than ever.

item.title: Drake Maye has to step up – but not how you might think | Opinion
item.description: With A.J. Brown injured, the Patriots need Drake Maye to step up – but not by having the quarterback play hero for the offense.
item.content:encoded:
The New England Patriots' season-opening loss left the reigning AFC champions with an uncomfortable air of familiarity.

The narrow defeat to the Seattle Seahawks was hardly as lopsided as February's Super Bowl 60 shellacking. Yet for a team that made a concerted effort this offseason to address the undeniable deficiencies that became glaring in the title bout, the rematch resurfaced many of the same problems.

Seahawks coach Mike Macdonald again vexed New England on multiple fronts. The ground game never got going, and the Patriots' passing attack was thrown off by Seattle's incessant pressure. Above all, though, the Seahawks again broke the game open on critical late turnovers by Maye, with three fourth-quarter interceptions this time derailing the bid for revenge.

Putting yet another crushing collapse behind them would have been difficult enough for the Patriots on its own. But when it was revealed that wide receiver A.J. Brown would be placed on injured reserve and likely miss four to six weeks after spraining his ankle, an offense that became so rooted in his presence now looked potentially unmoored.

Addressing the loss on WEEI's "Jones & Keefe" on Friday, Sept. 11, Patriots offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels went as far as saying that moving forward without Brown would require an "all-hands-on-deck" approach. McDaniels conceded that no one player could replicate what the three-time Pro Bowler, who was brought on to provide Maye easier answers both in the vertical game and in the face of pressure, can offer the offense.

Where, then, does that leave Maye heading into Sunday's showdown with the Pittsburgh Steelers?

Trying to leverage his considerable playmaking talents to ignite big plays would be a natural response for any young quarterback facing a similarly problematic outlook on the perimeter. Overcompensating, however, might be the worst thing that the runner-up for NFL MVP can do.

To not only navigate the absence of a gravitational force in the aerial attack but also take the next step in his evolution as a passer, Maye likely needs to focus on one trait above all: restraint.

Does Drake Maye need to be less aggressive? Not necessarily

For whatever disconnect emerged in the Patriots' late-game approach in the season opener, Maye and Patriots coach Mike Vrabel were on the same page about what drove the late breakdown after a workable start.

"I thought we had a good plan to try to start chipping away and be patient," Maye said after the game. "Lost patience and it cost us – decisions that cost us the game on my part, on my end. ... It's unacceptable."

Said Vrabel after the game: "You can’t throw three interceptions. Drake knows that."

Not being lured by big-play opportunities that quickly transformed into turnover traps was paramount to the game plan against Seattle. Maye complied for most of the contest, keeping New England in contention until his inexplicable heave to the end zone with less than 30 seconds remaining was brought down by Seahawks cornerback Josh Jobe, denying the Patriots their previously earned shot at an easy game-tying field goal.

Maye throwing all three picks once Brown had exited the game might sound the alarm for some. For the quarterback, though, his calamitous quarter should serve as a reminder of the need to play both within himself and the game plan.

Embracing a more cautious approach might seem like a way for New England to willfully box itself in after explosive plays fueled last year's second-ranked scoring offense. But Vrabel and Maye worded their reflections carefully. New England is intent on being more judicious without tilting into being overly conservative.

"That's what playing quarterback or playing in this league is all about," Vrabel said in a news conference on Sept. 16. " ... I think there's a difference between being reckless and being aggressive. We want to be aggressive. That's how we want to play.

"But we also have to make great decisions. When there's a look, maybe we take a certain play away."

With proper patience, opportunities for chunk gains should once again present themselves. They just might look a little different than they would with Brown in the lineup. New England wasn't particularly adept at capitalizing on contested catches last season, but Romeo Doubs could help the unit make substantial strides in that area. It's a skill set that surely could get the marquee free-agent signing more involved in the attack after he was held without a catch on three targets in the opener.

Above all, Maye has to embrace any opportunity to see another down when facing sufficient danger – something he eschewed late against Seattle.

When he harnesses the skill properly, Maye's proclivity for going big-game hunting can set him apart from his peers. But that focus – or drifting attention, as was the case in the season opener – also has worked to his severe detriment against top defenses in a different manner. His tendency to hold onto the ball past a point of safety colored a postseason run in which he took a record 21 sacks. His sky-high regular-season efficiency (highlighted by a 72% completion rate and league-leading 8.26 adjusted net yards per passing attempt) cratered in the playoffs, where he completed just 58.3% of his throws and registered a 4.5 ANY/A.

The temptation to sling his way back to the highs of his sophomore season could be strong, especially with the investments along the offensive line potentially affording him better protection against all non-Seahawks opponents further along on the schedule. But Maye is facing the challenge that any young quarterback on a similar star trajectory encounters. Like Patrick Mahomes and so many others before him, the third-year signal-caller now has defenses denying him the opportunity to throw over the top with any ease.

In sorting out how to move forward with his depleted receiving corps, operating with a reduced risk tolerance – at least to start – will be vital.

Revitalized run game could change everything

It's a fitting setup that this early potential inflection point for Maye and the Patriots comes against the Steelers.

In a 21-14 loss to Pittsburgh in Week 3 of last year, New England was plagued by many of the same ailments, including five sacks and five turnovers.

But as was the case against the Seahawks, another major shortcoming informed all aspects of the operation: a dead-on arrival run game.

Against the Steelers, the Patriots mustered just 74 yards on 22 carries from their running backs, with Maye providing life via his game-high 45 yards on the ground. In the loss to the Seahawks, lead ball carrier Rhamondre Stevenson had 10 of his 18 carries go for 3 yards or fewer. The net effect: Maye was repeatedly left in disadvantageous situations on second and third down, increasing the burden on him while allowing the Seahawks more freedom to tee off on him.

A pick-me-up, however, could be around the corner with the rushing attack.

Second-year back TreVeyon Henderson, who sat out the opener due to an ankle injury, returned to practice this week and is on track to play against Pittsburgh. His big-play flair as a rookie propped up an otherwise inert ground game, which ranked 25th in expected points added per rush even with his contributions.

Stevenson might still pace the attack, with Henderson's high variance as a runner and troublesome track record in blitz pickups working against him. But with Brown out and Maye trying not to force mistakes, New England might be inclined to turn back to the speedier back after his breakaway ability helped the offense tap into its explosive side down the stretch of the 2025 regular season.

The Patriots should also be confident that they won't find a team comparably adept at stuffing the run as the Seahawks, who last season surrendered the fewest yards per carry despite living in light boxes. For the Steelers, however, it's clear that shutting down that facet comes before teeing off on Maye.

"It's an issue only if we make it an issue," Steelers defensive tackle Cam Heyward said on "The Rich Eisen Show" on Sept. 15 when asked about Maye's recent turnover troubles. "As much as he turned the ball over, he's gonna try to overprotect the ball. But we have to get him in situations by stopping the run early, both first and second down, (and) controlling the play-action a lot more. ... (The turnovers) can't be a coincidence - we have to go out there and dominate from the get-go."

In taking accountability for his missteps, Maye on Wednesday returned to one of Vrabel's familiar refrains: "Be the conductor."

Vrabel previously used that nebulous term seemingly as a way to push Maye toward taking more control of the operation. At least until Brown is healed, though, the Patriots might find value in the less artistic definition, as they surely could use someone who keeps everything on schedule and gets them safely to their next stop.

If the conductor's hat fits, wear it.

item.title: Joe Brady: I wanted to take the ball in that environment and set the tone
item.description: Many teams choose to defer to the second half after winning the coin toss before games, but Bills head coach Joe Brady did not do that on Thursday night.
item.content:encoded:
Many teams choose to defer to the second half after winning the coin toss before games, but Bills head coach Joe Brady did not do that on Thursday night.

Brady elected to take the ball to start the first game at his team's new stadium and that turned out to be a wise move. Running back James Cook ran three times for 23 yards while quarterback Josh Allen completed two passes for 22 yards and ran four times for 40 yards, including a one-yard touchdown to set off a frenzied celebration in the team's new home.

"I've said all along, it was important for us, and I wanted to take the ball in this environment and set the tone," Brady said, via WGR. "I thought we had some good third downs, we finished in the end zone, and that stadium was electric. That was the start that we needed."

Brady was remembering another drive involving third downs because the Bills never faced one on that trip to the end zone, but that's understandable because his team had six touchdown drives over the course of the 41-31 win. All of that success can run together, especially when it plays out to a soundtrack of joyful Bills fans celebrating a memorable night in franchise history.

With Buffalo rolling and leading, 21-7, Allen threw into the end zone for Moore on second-and-3 from the 6-yard line. Moore, attempted to haul in a low pass, smashed his shoulder onto the grass, rolled to his back and grabbed around the left side of his collarbone.

Moore walked off under his own power to the locker room for X-rays.

It was Moore’s first target of the game, though it wasn’t recorded as one, as the Bills were flagged for offensive holding on the play. He did have a carry for a loss of a yard earlier in the game.

Sean McVay: Myles Garrett is like Wolverine, healing fast, but we won’t rush him back | Pro Football Talk

That doesn’t necessarily mean Garrett will be back on the field on October 18 for the Rams’ Week 6 game against the Cardinals, which is the earliest he’s eligible to return from injured reserve.

“I’m reluctant to put a timeline on it,” McVay said. “We know that he’s going to miss those four weeks at a minimum. We’re not going to rush him back. We want to make sure he’s feeling good, he’s able to get on the practice field, do all the things that are necessary for him to perform at a level that he’s been accustomed to. I’ll keep you guys posted as we have updates, as we go.”

In case you missed it on Arrowhead Pride

Numbers Never Lie: 3 Chiefs stats and what they mean for this season

The Chiefs generated pressure on 46% of dropbacks

That was the fourth-highest rate of any NFL team in Week 1, looking up in the rankings at only the Baltimore Ravens, Minnesota Vikings and Philadelphia Eagles. It’s a good group to be in.

The Chiefs blitzed on nearly one-third of the pass plays the team faced. However, when you take away those reps, Kansas City still generated pressure on 36% of pass plays. That ranked 10th among all NFL teams while rushing only four players.

The Cincinnati Bengals are coming off a serious high after Week 1, where their defense actually led them to victory. A far cry from what this team had to deal with the last few seasons. The four turnovers led directly to 24 of Cincinnati’s 27 points. That includes Demetrius Knight’s fumble recovery returned for a touchdown as the first score of the season for the Bengals.

Now a different test is on the horizon. The Houston Texans, with their ferocious pass rush, are ready to host Joe Burrow and company. The offense had a bit of a slow start against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, especially in Goal-to-Go situations. That will need to be cleaned up, as those opportunities may not be as plentiful against this defense.

We will have to see how for real these two teams are, as it will be an early litmus test for both.

Here is everything you need to watch the Bengals take on the Texans for Week 2.

How to Watch Bengals at Texans

  • Date/Time: September 20th at 1:00 pm ET
  • Location: Houston, Texas at Reliant Stadium
  • TV Channel: CBS
  • Broadcasters: Play-by-Play Kevin Harlan, analyst Trent Green, and sideline reporter Melanie Collins
  • Online Stream:Paramount+  (in market), NFL+ (in market), NFL Sunday Ticket (out of market), and NFL Game Pass International (International, excluding China)

  • ESPN: two of six experts (at the time of writing) are taking Cincinnati
  • CBS Sports: Two of the three experts (at the time of writing) are going with the Bengals

Cincy Jungle: The Texans defense is going to be the major worry here. That pass rush will really test this offensive line that has been rolling since Burrow’s return midway through 2025. They will certainly need more from Ja’Marr Chase, who was held to just two catches for 12 yards last week.

Then there is the Houston offense that is still led by CJ Stroud. He looked good, but he was sacked three times. Cincinnati’s defense blitzed at the lowest level of any defense in Week 1, but they got the 10th most pressure on quarterbacks. That means the coverage was solid while the defensive line has been showing off its improvements.

item.title: Broncos players react to ugly loss against Kansas City
item.description: Bo Nix, Pat Surtain II and Courtland Sutton reflected on Denver’s tough loss and what the Broncos must do going forward.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, Broncos Country!

Teams face adversity.

It’s not a matter of if, but when. For the Denver Broncos, it just happens to come a little earlier than some (most) would have liked. But how the Broncos respond to the beatdown at the hands of the Kansas City Chiefs this Sunday will reveal what kind of makeup they have.

To add to the motivation, Denver faces the Jacksonville Jaguars, a team that thoroughly whipped it 34-20 a season ago.

The good news is the Broncos have been in this position before under Sean Payton, going 4-8 in and struggling in September games heading into Sunday.

“I learned a long time ago, you never play as bad as you think and you never play as good as you think,” Broncos quarterback Bo Nix said to the media on Thursday. “So for us, it was the case of we didn’t play as bad as what we thought. We just there at the end of the game, we didn’t make third-down conversions. We felt like it was 7-7, 14-7, and 21-7 for a long time in the game. So it was reachable, and we were in it for a while.

“We just didn’t help ourselves by any means. You watch the film, and there are a couple good things and then all of a sudden we’re back because of a penalty or something. You just can’t win in this league like that. So, overall, we’re not going to press the panic button, and we’re not freaking out. We’re not starting from scratch or anything. We’re still in a good spot, and we just didn’t play great by any means, and we’ve got to play better.”

The first step to correcting what went wrong against the Chiefs is the work at practice this week. As Nix said after the game on Monday, it was a “nasty wake-up call.”

After that, it’s about the players doing their job, doing the little things, and executing.

“We all know we are a very talented team, no question about it,” Broncos cornerback Pat Surtain II said to the media. “That’s why I feel like everybody has us on the high horse and stuff like that. That comes with a certain privilege. But if you don’t show up each and every week, you’re going to get humbled quickly. Every week is a new challenge.

“We all know that as a team, but we just have to focus on getting better day-by-day and honing in on the small details. I think that’s what’s going to separate us. It’s still early in the year. Going into our second game, we know what we need to correct. Like I said before, every week’s a new challenge. You have to bring the intensity no matter what.”

If used properly, being served some humble pie can be a good thing.

“I think the biggest thing is learning from our mistakes from what we saw on film,” Broncos receiver Courtland Sutton said to the media on Thursday. “There were things that we did well, things that we didn’t do well. Being able to build on what we did well, make that last longer throughout the game, and minimize our mistakes. I would say one of the things I’ve seen from the team over the past few days, since the game, is an attitude of accountability, an attitude of wanting to get better and improving so that we can maximize these days leading up into Jacksonville.”

Teams face adversity; it’s a matter of how they respond. Denver gets its first test on Sunday.

What can certainly help the Broncos is playing at home.

“A big spark,” Nix said when asked about the spark Broncos Country could provide. “There’s nothing like a home-field advantage, nothing like playing at home. I know, as an away team, what it’s like to go and play in a loud environment. It’s definitely not easy. There are a lot of variables and things that go into it, a lot of communication tactics. It’s just not easy, and that’s what the crowd does. The crowd makes it not easy for them.

“So hopefully we’ll have, like we always do, a sellout, hopefully we’ll have a loud environment, and I expect it to be a really fun time being the home opener. I expect it to be loud. Essentially, what it is, it’s a playoff game. So I expect it to be that kind of environment, sort of like we had at the end of the season last year.”

item.content:encoded:
Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories as the Giants get set for their Monday night game against the Los Angeles Rams.

Why NFL offenses are going under center more often in 2026 | ESPN.com

Giants fans who were trepidatious about the additions of Matt Nagy and Greg Roman as offensive architects have to feel great about what they saw in Week 1. The Giants were the league’s second-best offense during the opening week of the season by EPA per play, trailing only the Bears. Their 58% success rate was second behind the Jaguars. The only reason they didn’t score more points was time; the Giants used more time per play than anybody else in the league and had only seven possessions in their 28-20 victory over Dallas.

As a passer, Dart didn’t have a huge game working from under center, going 5-of-7 for 39 yards with a 2-yard touchdown pass to Isaiah Likely. In all, though, the Giants looked comfortable majoring under center, something they ran only 20% of the time while Dart was on the field a year ago. It’s a positive sign for their offensive progress, although the Rams might offer a more imposing defense to Dart this week on “Monday Night Football.”

Dart, Likely keys to impressive win: NFL Insider

How this Giants star got on same page with Jaxson Dart and earned his trust | The Record

The scene was common on the practice fields with the New York Giants all summer.

Starting in West Virginia and continuing in New Jersey, seemingly every day of training camp, Jaxson Dart and Isaiah Likely would be standing together talking football. They would chat up different route concepts, the rules to follow for offscript plays and, above all else, gain comfort in the trust between them.

Rams’ Aaron Donald returning vs. Giants? Here’s what Jaxson Dart thinks of facing him | NJ.com

Dart said Donald’s “real impact on the game” — beyond his 111 sacks, eight first-team All-Pro selections and three Defensive Player of the Year awards — stems from how offenses must scheme around him.

“For the longest time that I can remember, he’s one of the most dominant players that I’ve watched,” Dart said. “So getting the chance to go out there and compete against him, it’s going to be really cool, just to be on the same field as him. He’s a great player, and I’ve heard that he’s kept himself in really good shape. So it’s going to be a great competition. There’s countless clips of putting three offensive linemen on him and [Donald] still being able to make a play. So he’s an unbelievable player and has had an unbelievable career.”

Dru Phillips tells The Post how he’s going to turn penalty-filled Week 1 into ‘learning point’ | New York Post

Players always say they need to clean up whatever mistakes they made in one game before they hit the field for the next game. Dru Phillips is in that mode this week. 

The third-year cornerback was called for three pass interference penalties in the season-opening 28-20 victory over the Cowboys.

Why it was so important for Giants to secure signature win early in John Harbaugh’s tenure | The Athletic

Harbaugh’s resume gave him instant credibility throughout the organization and in the locker room. But the buy-in could fade if the results don’t follow the hard work. That’s why Sunday’s impressive start has made the Giants even stronger believers in Harbaugh’s methods.

“I don’t think anyone would shy away from saying it was the hardest training camp of their career,” 10th-year veteran right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor said. “I’ve been around Harbs (in Baltimore), and this was a physical-ass training camp. Now you know why you run that many plays in practice, why you hit as much, why you do those practices, why you lift as much as we do, how hard we work because you go out there on Sunday and, you really beat a team up like that.”

NFL Take-o-Meter: What’s Real and Not Entering Week 2 | The Ringer

[Extremely John Harbaugh voice] The New York GIANTS are legit contenders. I’ll admit it! I was overconfident that the Giants would stumble out of the gate. I (like an idiot) was high on the Cowboys offense and expected Dallas to experience some positive defensive regression after letting Matt Eberflus loose and replacing him at DC with football nerd icon Christian Parker. But Harbaugh’s new disgusting brothers in the booth— offensive coordinator Matt Nagy and assistant Greg Roman —took out a paddle and spanked the silver off the Cowboys’ pants for all to see.

I’m a believer in the tone the Giants want to set and Skattebo’s ability to set it, but I am not buying fully in just yet. The only defense worse than Big Blue’s in Week 1 (again, by EPA per drive) was Parker’s disasterclass. Let’s see Harbaugh and his guys throw the same haymakers against the Rams with Sean McVay and Co. in a must-win spot coming off their Melbourne embarrassment. 

Daniel Jones lost a friend to suicide; now he advocates for others to ask for help | The Athletic

Mission 34’s motto, “A New Type of Tough,” was painted on Jones’ cleats. The five-word slogan is aimed at those who may be struggling with their mental health, especially athletes, with the goal of helping them realize that toughness isn’t defined by a lack of vulnerability, the Bonners said. They believe, along with Jones, that there is strength — and life — in speaking up. Last November wasn’t the first time Jones teamed up with Mission 34, having represented the organization during his New York Giants days, and it won’t be his last. Jones considers it a worthy cause, and he’s keenly aware of the NFL spotlight he wields.

September is National Suicide Prevention Month, If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, call or text 988 for the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, or contact the Crisis Text Line by texting HOME to 741741.
